title: Luong et al. (2011): True or False
instructions: Choose True or False, then use the explanation and source passage to check the scope of the evidence and its exceptions.

items.prompt: Older adults tend to report greater satisfaction and more positive experiences in their social relationships than younger adults do.
items.explanation: The review describes reports of better-quality ties with children, more positive marriages, closer friendships, and fewer negative social experiences among older adults. These are general patterns in the findings, not a claim that every individual has the same experience.

items.prompt: The article concludes that smaller social networks in later life arise primarily because friends and family members die.
items.explanation: The authors attribute the main age differences in network composition to proactive efforts to reduce less-close ties and maintain close relationships. They do not identify deaths of social partners as the primary explanation for those differences.

items.prompt: In SST, chronological age directly determines social goals, and perceptions of remaining time are unimportant.
items.explanation: SST emphasizes temporal horizons: how people perceive the time left in their lives. These perceptions shape motivational goals at all ages; age is associated with a shorter horizon but is not a substitute for the proposed time-perspective mechanism.

items.prompt: In the research discussed in the review, the same positivity bias described among older adults was not observed among younger adults.
items.explanation: The article describes older adults' tendency to attend to positive experiences and avoid negative ones as a positivity bias. It explicitly states that the same bias was not observed in younger adults in the cited research.

items.prompt: The finding that highly socially active younger adults made trait-diagnostic judgments similar to older adults supports a possible contribution of social experience.
items.explanation: The authors interpret this finding as evidence that social experiences contribute to judgments about potential partners. It supports considering accumulated experience when explaining social expertise, rather than treating chronological age alone as the explanation.

items.prompt: When younger and older adults used the same strategy to avoid an argument, only older adults reported reduced emotional reactivity.
items.explanation: The two age groups were equally emotionally reactive when they engaged in arguments. When they used the same avoidance strategy, however, only older adults reported less reactivity, showing that the benefit depended on the response to the conflict.

items.prompt: Retirement and an empty nest can change older adults' social environments by reducing interpersonal demands associated with work and childcare.
items.explanation: The article identifies greater freedom to choose partners and leisure activities after retirement, along with reduced full-time employment and childcare demands, as possible structural paths to fewer interpersonal stressors. These possibilities depend on social roles and living arrangements.
items.source: Structural changes in the social environment

items.prompt: SIM explains only older adults' individual emotion regulation and excludes the responses of their social partners.
items.explanation: The Social Input Model emphasizes dynamic, reciprocal interactions. Older adults may enhance the positive qualities of relationships, and their partners may reciprocate with kindness and responses that reduce tension.

items.prompt: For the same social faux pas, respondents endorsed more direct confrontation when the offender was an older adult than when the offender was a younger adult.
items.explanation: In the vignette study, respondents were more likely to predict disengagement and conflict avoidance toward an older offender. They endorsed more direct communication or confrontation toward a younger offender. These were judgments about hypothetical responses.

items.prompt: In a naturalistic study in which adults aged 20 to 87 submitted holiday cards they had received, older adults' cards contained more personal and sentimental messages.
items.explanation: The holiday-card study examined cards people actually received. Separate birthday-card selection research similarly found a greater tendency to choose personal or sentimental messages for older recipients.

items.prompt: Participants who imagined that their remaining time with a social partner was limited chose to avoid arguments with that partner.
items.explanation: In hypothetical situations that shortened time with close younger or older partners, participants reported that they would avoid arguments. They endorsed more direct confrontation with younger partners who were not moving away and with whom more time remained.

items.prompt: Negative stereotypes about aging always led to harsher punishment and less sympathy for older adults.
items.explanation: When an older woman's intentions were ambiguous, a stereotype of forgetfulness was associated with less blame and punishment. In another study, stereotypes of slowing in later life could evoke greater sympathy for older workers. The review therefore describes cases in which negative stereotypes accompanied more favorable treatment.

items.prompt: U.S. studies consistently found that greater respect for an older partner who committed a social transgression was associated with more favorable treatment of that partner.
items.explanation: The review describes less consistent U.S. findings and reports that respect for the older offending partner was not related to more favorable treatment. It separately discusses cultural settings in which respect and filial piety may contribute to deference toward older adults.

items.prompt: The authors argue that small social networks can never create problems for emotional well-being in later life.
items.explanation: Problems can arise when a network becomes too small to meet social needs. Older adults reporting fewer than three close partners also reported less social embeddedness and satisfaction, and greater loneliness. The review does not treat every small network as equally adequate.

items.prompt: The authors state that cohort effects cannot be ruled out for the sentimental-card findings and some other evidence supporting SIM.
items.explanation: Earlier generations may have had stronger norms of sending thoughtful cards, which could help explain why older recipients received more sentimental messages. The authors call for further research to separate cohort explanations from the processes proposed by SIM.
